findings.title: The clock-POSITION invariant is pinned for only one of the four writers: moving regenerateAsk’s and settleGenerationExhaustion’s decision instant inside their transactions, after the advisory-lock wait, passes all 23 promised tests
findings.reason: The intake’s FIRST invariant is lane-wide: "The clock is read immediately after the render DECISION and before the transaction opens or waits ... Round 1 rejected the earlier design, which read the clock inside the transaction and made both columns persist time." The only test that measures POSITION rather than column equality — "the render lane never stamps occurred_at from the transaction, so a slow lock does not move the decision time" — drives generateAsksForBatch, so it exercises persistChildRender (W1, and W2 through it) and neither of the other two writers. M14 and M15 each restored exactly the rejected design for one writer and were invisible to the whole suite. Column equality survives the mutation because rendered_at and occurred_at move together, which is precisely why the equality tests (I3) cannot stand in for a position test. Suggested closure: extend the held-advisory-lock fixture (holdBatchAdvisoryLock, already in the suite) to regenerateAsk and settleGenerationExhaustion, asserting the same rendered_at_ms < lockHeldAt + HOLD_MS discriminator that kills M1 today.
findings.arbiter_reasoning: NOT equivalent: the mutation changes what solicitation_outreach.rendered_at and refusal_events.occurred_at record, from decision time to post-advisory-lock persist time. That is the exact semantic difference the intake records as decided and the production comments at both sites assert ("before this transaction opens or waits on the advisory lock"). NOT an unexecuted branch: both mutated statements lie on the straight-line path of transactions that the passing integration tests drive — I6 ("a generation exhaustion writes one refusal_events row per outreach hole") reaches the settleGenerationExhaustion statement and I7 ("a regenerated ask writes its refusal_events row against the replacement outreach id") reaches the regenerateAsk statement; both wrote their rows under the mutation, so the line executed and produced a differently-timestamped row that no assertion inspected. Contrast with M8, which I DID reclassify as unexecuted after M10 proved the fixture aborts earlier; no such reclassification applies here, and M1 demonstrates the suite CAN kill this mutation class when the probe is aimed at the one writer it covers.

findings.title: Two guard mutations turn the unit suite red through mock-SQL FIFO exhaustion rather than through the behavioural assertion
findings.reason: Deleting the outbox-ownership CAS (M5) or the batch-lifecycle re-check (M6) makes the run throw "batch ... vanished before child persist" / "... before the finale" — the mutant consumed queue entries the fixture did not provision — so the trailing expect(writeRefusalEvent).not.toHaveBeenCalled() never evaluates. The tests are NOT hollow: M7 and M10, which leave every guard intact and hoist only the ledger write above the guard, were killed on that exact assertion, so the property is genuinely measured. Recorded because the coarse channel means these two rows would also go red for many changes unrelated to the ledger, which weakens them as regression pins. No action required for this PR.

findings.title: The cross-writer matrix test pairs the Nth ledger call with the Nth withheld insert positionally
findings.reason: refusalCalls()[i] is matched to withheld[i] by array index across four separately-driven writers. This is sound TODAY — every call site writes its Refusal synchronously immediately after its own insert on a sequential path, so call order is a real contract, not an incidental one — and it is not the fragile-assertion class the skill names (no tag proxy, no exact string count, no ordering assertion over an unordered source). Recorded only because the coupling is implicit: were any writer ever to batch or reorder its inserts, this test would fail for a reason unrelated to what it names. subjectId is separately pinned by identity (inserts.indexOf), which is the part that carries the real weight.
